in_text_mentions: During physical examination, unexpectedly, bilateral preauricular fistulas and anterior cervical fistulas were found (Fig. 2A, B, C and D). Preauricular fistulas were congenital while anterior cervical fistulas were noticed at the age of 5. Examination (detail in Table 1) revealed proteinuria of 39.0 ~ 68.9 mg/kg/d and renal insufficiency. Tests for autoimmune diseases or infection were negative. Area under the curve of MMF was 47.6 µg.hr/mL (reference range: 20 ~ 60). At admission, branchial and otic scars were not noticeable, but branchial and preauricular pits of his brother was informed (Fig. 2E and F). Examinations revealed azotemia, hyperuricemia (uric acid of 533.8 µmol/L) and anemia (hemoglobin of 103 g/L). Urinary analysis revealed proteinuria of 31.9 mg/kg/d (detail in Table 1). Ultrasound revealed small kidneys, lacking distinct cortical–medullary demarcation. According to the diagnostic criteria for BOR syndrome presented by Chang et al., if there is a family history, the diagnosis can be made when one or more of the main diagnostic criteria, including branchial cleft anomaly, deafness, preauricular pits, and renal anomaly, are meant [5]. Therefore, this case was suitably diagnosed as BOR syndrome; the patient had a family history of two types of branchial cleft anomalies and preauricular pits. Figure 1 shows the patient’s pedigree. Figure 2 and Figure 3 show the patient’s bilateral branchial cysts, fistula openings, and preauricular pits.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Fetal ultrasound panel showing small left kidney with decreased volume in fetus with Branchio-oto-renal syndrome per disease-focused article title and caption; corresponds to renal hypoplasia vocabulary term. B: Fetal ultrasound panel showing small right kidney with decreased volume in fetus with Branchio-oto-renal syndrome per disease-focused article title and caption; corresponds to renal hypoplasia. C: Follow-up fetal ultrasound showing persistently decreased left kidney volume in BOR fetus; caption and in-text specify decreased volume and increased echo. D: Follow-up fetal ultrasound showing persistently decreased right kidney volume in BOR fetus; caption and in-text specify decreased volume and increased echo.
panels.attribution_text: Tang et al. Prenatal diagnosis and genetic analysis of a fetus with Branchio-oto-renal syndrome: A case report.. Medicine 2022. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000031172. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Ultrasound image of fetal kidney. A, B: Left and right kidney size at 33 weeks + 4 days; renal volume decreased and echo increased; C, D: 36 weeks + 3 days, the volume of both kidneys decreased and the echo increased.
in_text_mentions: metaphase, 2 ultrasounds showed that good fetal heart and fetal movement, but did not indicate the size of both kidneys. At the 33 + 4 weeks of pregnancy, ultrasound examination showed that the size of the left kidney was 21*12 mm (–5.09 SD, average longitudinal diameter is 44.72 mm), the anteroposternal diameter of the left renal pelvis was 6.7 mm, and the size of the right kidney was 31*23 mm (–2.94 SD) (Fig. 1A, B). The echo of both kidneys was slightly stronger, and the amniotic fluid volume was normal. Ultrasound examination of adult urinary system of fetal parents showed no abnormality.

After 3 weeks, the ultrasound amniotic fluid index was 133 mm, the left kidney size of the fetus was 24*13 mm (–4.65 SD), and the size of the right kidney was 31*23 mm (–3.17 SD). The echo of both kidneys was slightly stronger, the bilateral renal arteries and the bladder were visible (Fig. 1C, D).

findings.label: Branchial cleft cyst
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Bilateral second branchial cysts and fistulas opening'; yellow circles mark the bilateral second branchial fistula openings on the lateral neck.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a BOR syndrome patient's neck showing bilateral second branchial cyst/fistula openings, highlighted by yellow circles with text annotation. Branchial cleft anomalies are a main diagnostic criterion of BOR syndrome per the in-text discussion of the Chang criteria, and the in-text mentions attribute Figure 2 to this patient. This is a classic branchial cleft anomaly presentation of BOR syndrome; image is somewhat grainy but the findings are visible and the prior triage kept it. No subtype is supported by the provided vocabulary, and no age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text.

panels.figure_caption: Bilateral second branchial cysts and fistulas opening.
in_text_mentions: tomatic. According to the diagnostic criteria for BOR syndrome presented by Chang et al., if there is a family history, the diagnosis can be made when one or more of the main diagnostic criteria, including branchial cleft anomaly, deafness, preauricular pits, and renal anomaly, are meant [5]. Therefore, this case was suitably diagnosed as BOR syndrome; the patient had a family history of two types of branchial cleft anomalies and preauricular pits. Figure 1 shows the patient’s pedigree. Figure 2 and Figure 3 show the patient’s bilateral branchial cysts, fistula openings, and preauricular pits.
